utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear now? Yes. I was saying that I was greeting the accused, Mr. Praljak, first of all, since he is testifying, the Defence counsel, Mr. Khan, who has replaced Mr. Karnavas in his seat, Mr. Stringer and all his associates, as well as all the people assisting us. I shall now give the floor to Ms. Pinter, who will resume her examination-in-chief of Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We'll, let's be as efficacious as possible. We're dealing with a binder relating to effective control, and please look at 3D01193. 1193, for the record, please, 3D01193. General, can you tell us something about this document, the circumstances under which it was written and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says in the document here, in the night between the 30th of April and 1st of May, 1992, at 1.00 a.m., 0100 hours, I was stopped by a policeman in Ljubuski in 1992. He was drunk, and I reported him. So that's what I want to say. The document speaks for itself, and I claim that I reported everything that I considered to be out of order and contrary to the rules and regulations, and that such conduct was unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And was it according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't have a police officer under the influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now look at the video. 3D03114 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, when we take a look at the video, could you tell us what it is about, when it was filmed, if you can remember, and the circumstances, and what this meeting was? For the record, the number of the video is 3D03563, so I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Soldiers, officers, non-commissioned officers, thank you for attending the solemn oath that you've taken. There's no smoking here during this official ceremony, so put your cigarettes off -- out. The idea of the people is a great idea. This rally is going to last for 25 minutes, so please stand at attention. "There are people who are much older than us, more numerous than us, or people and nations older than us, so we must devote all our efforts to the state ideal and idea of our nation. We are parents of the child which is that idea and ideal, so bear that in mind when you're digging trenches, when you're looking after your weapons, when you're out in the streets, behaving during your daily lives. "Happy Christmas to you all, Happy New Year. May you be blessed and happy, and please remember those friends of yours who are no more. "Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, can you tell us something about that video and something about your speech delivered at that rally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in 1992, just before Christmas, in Zenica, when a brigade was being established, the Jure Francetic HVO Brigade, and as you were able to see, my speech is very short and to the point, very clear. So, first of all, this is a rally of volunteers that have reported to the HVO, and it will take them some time to become proper soldiers, the kind of soldier that exists in the West. And I state right at the outset here -- I'm telling them that -- well, I wouldn't change anything in that speech of mine. I, first of all, told them that they weren't allowed to smoke while they were standing to attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the first time I see this video. I've seen a lot of videos, but I wasn't familiar with this one. We saw the images go by very quickly. It seems that I saw, among the soldiers, a young boy holding a flag. Were there children in the troops of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Perhaps they just put a little boy there to hold up the flag. But as far as I know, and I knew a lot of HVO soldiers, of course, none of them were under the age of 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the beginning, and perhaps you'll be able to give a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the point. This was a detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I have to ask you this. You say it's not easy to win a state, to get a state?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I said a state cannot be gained that easily, and that the state is the mother, and everybody asks something of their mother. And I say that an idea and an ideal is like a child, so I turn the whole thing the other way 'round. You have to look after your child, tell your child how to behave in the streets, how to clean weapons, how to dig, and so on. And how well they're able to do that is how attached to the ideal of the Croatian people they are, and if they work with a lot of discipline, then the idea and ideal of the Croatian nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina will be realised. So I stand by what I said then, and I state again -- or, rather, I stated again that there must be law and order, and I stipulate what somebody who wants to be in the HVO should do and how they must act.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So you were actually building up a Croatian state in that area; would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about the ideas and ideals of the Croatian people on that territory. You can't mention any state there. We're not mentioning any state there, just the survival and ideals of the Croatian nation on that territory. And it was a territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what the fate of the Croatian nation will be there will depend on how ready they are to fight for it, because the Serbs were not far away from Zenica by this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask, perhaps with the assistance of the interpreters, what terms are used for "state," because just now Mr. Praljak says there's no mention of a state; and on line 15, he speaks about the state. So were there different terms in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the video played again? I think that would be the best thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Gentlemen, soldiers, junior officers, officers, I congratulate you on taking the solemn oath to your people. You were praised, gentlemen, soldiers, junior officers, and officers, in a formation, and while taking the solemn oath, you are not to smoke."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I say, no smoking, throw your cigarettes away. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Gentlemen, the ideal of the nation is a great ideal, and it's not as cold as you think it is, neither is this meeting going to last too long. It will last 20 minutes, so we can sacrifice for that ideal our cigarettes and stand to attention."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying there is they are not to smoke.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Take into consideration that there are nations which are older than ours, not greater than ours, but more numerous than ours."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I mention the state here, but I am talking about the state on whose soil they are, and that is to say Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are nations that are older than ours, and of course I meant the Kurds there and many other nations and peoples who have an older civilization, thousands of years of civilization, and still have not been able to have their own state. And I don't divide nations into big, large nations, or small, but into numerous nations and those which are less numerous. That's what I say. But I don't recognise that great nations exist and small nations exist. It's just a question of population, nations with a larger population and with a smaller population. Now we can play the video further.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "You must dedicate yourself to the ideal of a state every day. The idea and ideals of a state is not a mother but a child to which every single one of us is a parent who must consider how to help this ideal instead of how to take advantage of it."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here I say that this idea and ideal of a nation means --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: General Praljak is kindly asked not to speak at the same time as the video is being played. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Bear that in mind when you're digging --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: General Praljak, do not speak when the video is on. They cannot follow you and also the video. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "As much as we are ready to give and accept this idea, the idea of the Croatian nation shall remain in existence for that long."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I am saying that if they devote themselves to that ideal and idea, and the extent to which they are able to devote themselves to it, that will be the extent to which it will survive in those parts. I think that the speech is very clear, and there's no dilemma about what I'm saying with respect to law and order, the survival, and idea of survival, and so on and so forth. And when I mention the state over there, I meant the state in which they were, and that was Zenica 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Merry Christmas and a very Happy New Year. God bless you and good luck. Remember your friends who are with us no longer."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There, at the end, I wish them Merry Christmas, and I say that when you think times are hard, just remember those friends who are with us no longer, because it's war, it's 1992, and people have already been killed. So if you remember those people who have been killed, you will gain the strength to fight further. So I have nothing more -- that's it. I have nothing more to add to this video, and I'm open for questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just as we are invited to ask questions: Mr. Praljak, there are a number of persons dressed in white in the back. Do they belong to the medical personnel? Are they sanitary troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, I can't tell you exactly at this point in time. I can't say. As far as I remember -- let me just add, I can't say for sure, but I seem to remember that we had members of the BH Army there as guests. And as for the white uniforms, it's not the Medical Corps, it's that we expected snow to fall. So some units wore this uniform by way of camouflage in the snow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I may have missed this. Could you give us the date when this was taken, the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before Christmas 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, look at 3D01168 now, please. 1168, just two 1s. 3D01168 is the correct number. Can you tell us something about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was written while I was in Central Bosnia. There was a unit there commanded by Darko Kraljevic from Vitez, and we had trouble with that unit with respect to military discipline. They did not follow orders and so on and so forth. So I asked Mr. Stojic here -- and this was a special-purpose unit, and they didn't listen to General Blaskic, so I say they should be sanctioned until they obey orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, General, what was your relationship towards lack of discipline or soldiers who had committed a crime or offence of some kind and something contrary to the rules and laws?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Nika, I punished soldiers for transgressions, but I didn't have any contact with soldiers who had committed crimes or criminal acts. A report would be filed, proceedings initiated through the courts, and then they would be sentenced and serve prison terms, whether it was a murder, killing, or whatever. But lack of discipline and infractions of that kind were sanctioned and punished as much as we could, but I did -- I punished them more by talking to them, in verbal form. I would give them a good talking to. Now, you can't punish 50 soldiers, 50 people. They were all smoking, for example. There were civilians, and yesterday -- and it would take them a long time to become proper soldiers, so you can't really punish them for smoking. You have to try and prevail upon them in some other way and give them a hard talking to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at document 3D01073, please. The date is the 4th of April, 1993 -- the 6th of April, 1993. It is signed by Colonel Miro Andric, and we've already mentioned him in court here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time in April, as I've already said, I was down there, I would spend a few days down there. And this is a report by him. He's just reporting on the situation, and he sent me this report, too, because at that time I took part in talks on military and political problems and why some of the units of the brigade didn't want to take up their positions. So there were problems in the municipality, and the feedback between the civilian authorities and the military authorities. And, anyway, they were rebelling at this point in time, and so we had to deal with the situation. And I said that Mr. Stojic took part there, Miro Andric and I, myself, but Mr. Andric was not able to resolve this problem with the municipality; so we had to deal with it. I dealt with it at a meeting, and Mr. Stojic also had a meeting with them. It went on for quite a long time. And then we looked at what was happening up at the front-lines, at the defence lines, so that is what this report is about. It speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You mentioned a meeting in Ljubuski which you had with the municipal government there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So that's the document, the document about the meeting that you testified about earlier; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 2 here, in particular, people are simply embittered by the fact that what I've been saying all along, this problem of this semi-voluntary nature of the army, everybody could go to Croatia or wherever as they saw fit. And now they're asking themselves, Well, what kind of a government do we have? Who's in authority here? And why some people have to fight for their homes and for their families and for the homes and families of those who had fled. And then there were different ideas; that their property should be seized, that a law should be passed entitling people. Well, of course it's not -- it was not possible, but people were very bitter. And at one point, they simply said, Well, we're not going out in the field. Let them come and let them burn everything. Of course, these are not problems of an army as it is known, but these are the problems that you have if you have a structure that we had down there, and that's -- well, at the same time, an army is being construed as are the authorities, and nothing is really functioning. And then a small -- a small-scale discontent can grow into mutiny. And, again, you cannot deal with it with any kind of military orders, purely speaking. It simply does not function.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That is the time when we're still talking about the war and the conflicts with the Republika Srpska Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at 3D02616. The date is the 26th of July, 1993, the time when you were officially the commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the commander of the brigade from Posusje, Colonel Andjelko Djerek, is writing a report about the soldiers from the Independent Battalion of Novi Travnik going absent without leave. So these were people who had fled from Novi Travnik. And, well, he says that quite a lot of them fled to parts unknown, probably to Croatia, that there were 380 civilians in a camp near Posusje, and that there are no conscripts there who could be drafted into the unit. And he provides some figures here and so on, saying that that night they left their accommodation in the elementary school and simply fled. So the same thing that Judge Antonetti had asked me about, whether these were volunteers who remained in the classical sense of the word, such as the situation was in the USA at the beginning of the Second World War, some people volunteered and others remained behind. And here the term "volunteer" is a different -- has a different meaning. If those who can flee flee and are not punished, then all of them who remain are volunteers. And if some of them try to draft -- to dodge the draft, then you can use the military police to press them into their units. But if they don't like it, they can just cross the border. The border could be crossed at 1.000 locations. It was not a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to look at document P03734. It's a document dated the 27th of July, 1993. It is signed by Zlatko Senkic, from the Command of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, and this pertains to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is yet another -- well, we haven't seen so many here before, unfortunately. It's a classical way in which a report is submitted, that disciplinary proceedings were instituted against Brdar, and that he actually aimed his weapon at the commander of the 1st Battalion, and that he was punished with 15 days in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, this report was sent to whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the commander of the Central Bosnia Operation Zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But not to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there was no need for the Main Staff to get this kind of thing. It would just generate a lot of paper. These are the duties that are performed by the brigade commander, and this remains at the brigade command level. Perhaps it goes up to the operational zone command, but it did not concern the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have a difficult question for you. Since you are an intellectual, you'll understand. Without a doubt, through the swaths of documents we have seen, a reasonable trier of fact can see that there was a problem inside the HVO as regarded the conscripts or the volunteers, because a lot of them clearly didn't want to go out and fight. This is a real problem which I shall mention in two weeks' time. I shall mention a document which relates to a meeting between Bobetko, Tudjman and Susak, where this particular question was raised. So this was a real problem. A reasonable trier of fact tries to analyse the reasons for this, and one of the reasons, but this is just an assumption I'm submitting to you, could it be that the soldiers didn't feel they were engaged in a patriotic war, in the sense that a patriotic war symbolises the republican and secular values; but they were engaged in a nationalistic war in which, in which, the famous General de Gaulle said - who is a general like you - nationalism amounts to the hatred of others? In the end, all the soldiers that dropped out, didn't they feel that they were patriots who needed to fight, and this fight, one wanted them to engage in, was not a fight they identified with? What do you think about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, the problem is not that simple, and I will try to analyse it here. In a war, there is a congruence of a large number of things. Let me say first that nationalism could be qualified this way or that way. There is a word, "chauvinism," "jingoism," to describe hatred towards others. In many books on political science, nationalism is defined as increased love for one's own country and not hatred towards the other nations. So we don't know what term to use instead of "nation" and "nationalism" for something that might denote love. But that aside, you know, Judge Antonetti, that out of love for one's own country, the French -- after the Second World War, the French Resistance summarily executed at least 7.000 to 10.000 collaborators. That was done out of love. Well, it's very difficult, but what we have here is this: It's not true that these people did not feel the desire to fight for their own country, and it's Bosnia and Herzegovina in this case. This is a wider problem. First, this country broke down. They did not have a clear goal, what this country is, the country they are supposed to fight for. At the beginning, the goal was clear: Bosnia-Herzegovina. But you will see from texts by Franjo Tudjman and so on, as the war progressed, and the embargo was not lifted, and Serbs were allowed by the international community and so on, people starting asking themselves if it has already been decided somewhere, then what should I fight for? This was a problem that Franjo Tudjman and all of us who talked about that faced. If somebody lifts the embargo, and let's the Serbs massacre you and fight you in that way, then the question is: Isn't your fight in vein, because the maps have already been drawn somewhere? And you know how maps were drawn, in Versailles, at Yalta, in Kosovo, and so on. When the might -- or when the great powers decide things will be like this or like that, and people feel that something strange is going on, well, that's the first problem. The second problem was that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic didn't want to go out with a proposal for the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. People wanted to know. Well, Your Honour, life is very valuable to people who are 20 or 21 years old. What are they supposed to lie down their lives for, for what idea; the idea that 70 percent of the territory is held by the Serb Republic, that the international community has been tolerating all the way down to Srebrenica, or the idea of Alija Izetbegovic, that everybody has read, that this should be a state, a unitary state, where he -- with his 50 percent of the population would be in the majority? And then these people are asking themselves, Well, why should I get killed? I would prefer to flee to Croatia and save my life, and I will find some other place to live. So that's the second thing. And the third thing is those enclaves were scattered all over the place, and it was very difficult to link them up. In other words, the people from Livno wanted to defend Livno. People from Tomislavgrad wanted to defend Tomislavgrad. And people from Jajce fought well in Jajce, but when they lost Jajce and when everything was burnt down there and when they were expelled, they, as a group in disarray, an army in disarray, troops in disarray, did not have this feeling that they should defend the territory around Tomislavgrad and then one day return to Jajce. It is difficult to achieve that in any army, and this was no exception. So this whole spectrum of human distress, pain, the ordeal, the suffering that people experienced, and if 30.000 people are expelled from Jajce and there are so many killed, people don't have this clear-cut idea of what they were fighting for. Unlike in Croatia where every soldier knew these are Croatian borders, and we will reach those borders. And that will be a state, a democratic state, a parliamentary state, a well-organised state. But in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the war is going on, everybody is just sitting back and watching, nobody gives you any weapons, and if you have a modicum of sense you will ask yourself, Well, why should I get killed? Has this been solved? This is why people speak about treason, about being sold out, because people get those figments of their fantasy and they say, Why isn't anybody helping me? Why do the Serbs get so much? I could go on on this topic, but you have to add to this, well, the ideal of patriotism. You, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you know how few Frenchmen participated in the resistance. The rest just sit back. People made wine, people drank Chateau, fortunately, and a small minority fought back. There were some French admirals who had a large fleet, and they preferred Hitler to Churchill, and then Churchill had to bomb them. Unfortunately, one cannot simplify. This whole problem is a very complicated sociological problem. And now when we talk about unrest, an expert will come. If you have a group of people, a neutral group of people, such as ourselves here, if you have a small research into the aggression among the people here in this small group and you reach a certain result, and here on our desk we have tennis rackets, Your Honours, if you were to take the same group and control the level of aggression --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the testimony. It's irrelevant and it's very far off the track, I think, from the President's question, and I suggest we get back to more pertinent issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you have really elaborated on my question, which was simple, which was to know why soldiers would not fight. You gave an explanation, and I concluded that this was connected to the situation prevailing then in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Maybe this gives us an opportunity to understand better, but we can revisit the issue later on; and we will, because this issue was discussed at the top level in Croatia by Tudjman, Bobetko, and Susak, because they thought it was a real problem. Yes, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, let us go back to this document. Okay, we're done with this document. Could you please look at document 3D00967. It is your document. It is not signed, but --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's my document, and I think that if we've already seen it, I have nothing to add to it. It speaks for itself. Members of the HVO must not stop and control and search UNPROFOR vehicles, and that's it. The convoys, of course, in paragraph 3, what is meant here is this part of the job must be done where the convoys are loaded, but that's what I wrote. It doesn't have anything to do with the army, but -- well, convoys should be checked at the point of origin, lest some contraband should be loaded, and then it should be checked, taken along appropriate routes, and routes -- and checks should also be done en route.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at 3D01145.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a document from Major General Petkovic, dated the 9th of August, 1993. Well, nothing. It's a clear document, it speaks for itself. I have nothing to add to it. Proper lists should be kept of the soldiers, NCOs, and officers; and those who went AWOL must be reported and listed, they must be punished. Well, the document speaks for itself. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you agree with this document that General Petkovic drafted then, not now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would sign this document. Obviously, General Petkovic was the number-two person in the Main Staff. He had the right to issue orders. I was the only person superior to him, so he couldn't exercise command over me, but he could exercise command over everybody else in the army. So I wouldn't challenge this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can move on to 3D01189. It's a document from Emil Harah. It's similar to, but not the same as the one we had before, and could you please say something about that document? It's from the time when you were the commander of the Main Staff, and is this document -- did this document reach you in the Main Staff at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did it reach you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did have such documents. I can't say whether it was this document, but I did receive documents of this kind from there. And I had an opportunity to read such documents that dealt with smuggling and so on. I can't tell you whether I saw this particular document, but similar documents that spoke about smuggling, and crimes, and other phenomena of that nature, yes, definitely. So I can't really tell you, yes, I saw this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in a few days' time I will show you a document that was published in the official journal, the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna, regarding military prosecutors. Under Article 27 -- I could have brought the document today, but I didn't. Article 27 says that the commander of a unit, at his level, and you in this case, when they are made aware of a crime, have to inform the military prosecutors thereof. It's written black and white. I'll show the document, and I'll remind you of your position, because you say this was not under your purview. But this text I'm going to show you is in perfect contradiction to what you said. Until then, together with your counsel, you may study that document. We'll return to this later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This notion of jurisdiction or competence over something, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I think there is a misunderstanding. Under an obligation to report, yes, he was. For example, I pull over a police officer who pulled over me, and then he is drunk. And that is proof that I'm reporting a drunk officer. I can't say that it's not in my jurisdiction if I'm the one actually reporting this person. I never said that. What is not under my jurisdiction is whatever happens after that, which is something that I don't know. If I report certain people who are smoking while standing to attention during the swearing-in ceremony, then it's under my jurisdiction; and I, in fact, did that in a number of different situations. But, for example, you find out that a house burned down somewhere because someone had set fire to it, and then you report that a house has burnt down, but between the fact that a house burned down and the tracking down of the perpetrator, there is an enormous grey area. One has to find out who it was who set fire to the house, and how is that sort of thing investigated? Someone gets killed in Paris, how do you investigate who the perpetrator is? About 15 percent of those are eventually tracked down. I think that's what the problem is about. We all know that someone set fire to a house, but someone, and then we report an unknown perpetrator. There. And what we're talking about here is someone is supposed to be pointing their finger at someone else and saying, It was you. No one is allowed to do that. But again, even if we're talking about a drunk police officer, it's not about a house that burned down, something that I reported, because I was pulled over by a drunk policeman. So that's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, can we please go to 3D01152. This is an order by Zarko Tole signed, however, by Matic on the 13th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yet another attempt, in the thick of fighting on the 13th of August, 1993, another day like that. There were fires along -- or firing along a 300-kilometre line. It was especially difficult in Mostar. They're trying to teach these people here how to do office work and how to keep it neat. I have nothing to add to this. A dead-line was set, a five- or six-day dead-line to teach people how to keep their binders, their lists, their log-books, how orders were to be drawn up properly. Needless to say, that is also to be considered a skill, and it's something that is actually taught in armies across the world. These people simply didn't know how to do that, and this was an attempt to bring order to that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D02584, 02584. That one is similar; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The date is the 14th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The previous day, I think there was an attack that was launched on Sector South, but there you see Mr. Petkovic and I co-signed this document. One of the things in an army like this is, for example, the Ascension Day on the 15th of August, and then all of the soldiers are trying to get themselves released so that they could go home and spend this day with their families. This was a customary thing, and it applied despite the fact that there was a war on, and they were now serving an army. It's an age-long custom. They felt particularly deprived because they weren't allowed to go back to their homes on that day, so Petkovic here is saying that they can't abandon their positions, that they had responsibility. Military police were blocking all the roads out because the attack had already commenced. It's a document that I co-signed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you didn't co-sign it today, did you? How come you say you co-signed it? Where is that signature? Where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I said I would co-sign it today. I consider it to be a normal document. That's what I'm saying, a good document. I didn't say that I co-signed it. I said that I would co-sign it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, Mr. Praljak, the record says that you said "I co-signed it," and that would be on line 20 of page 21. So I invite our Defences, who are converse with both languages, to carefully control and intervene immediately when they notice that there are discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, our interpreters had interpreted accurately, in a word-perfect manner, what General Praljak said. The meaning behind this, however, is a bit different. When we say "I co-signed this today," that means I agree with it. It's a phrase which must be interpreted in the proper way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked the document -- with previous documents, whether he agreed with documents signed by General Petkovic. When using this phrase, the general actually wanted to recognise the document as his own without necessarily meaning that the formally and physically co-signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The 28th of January, 3D01202.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of my orders. Alcohol was a large-scale problem, an enormous problem. This is a problem that one comes across in any war in any army. It's a longstanding tradition from World War I, especially to be found in Russian units, even in World War II, when people were given alcohol to consume, before going into battle, in order to boost their bravery. A war is always a situation of exceptional stress, and people are under a lot of strain, abnormal strain. So what do they do? They're off to a pub, and they try to vent their anger and frustration by using alcohol for that purpose. To be perfectly frank, I don't think there was any legal basis for me to pass a document like this. I don't think that I was legally entitled. That was the civilian aspect, obviously. As for everything else, I agree. The situation with the facilities there obviously does not translate into pressure on the government that might then take a decision, but it certainly exerted pressure on me, because I saw the soldiers there, I saw guns being pulled when people were in a pub, and there was a war going on. So what I'm doing here, in view of that, is that all the pubs were to be shut down across the area. This was something that was very dangerous, and it could no longer be maintained. Everybody was at their wit's end and very exhausted, mentally and physically, and then they went off and had a drink, which made everything even worse. I still agree with this order that I wrote back then, although I'm aware that there was no legal basis for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You were trying to pick the lesser evil; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, you might put it that way.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an IPD document addressed to Veso Vegar. It discusses the situation following the fall of Bugojno. My name is mentioned here in a favourable light, in terms of command. An intervention by General Praljak prevented the fall of Gornji Vakuf. Obviously, no man could manage this on his own, although I was the trigger who made others follow. Likewise, he states that the situation is improving, that the morale is on its way up, and the belief in one's own strength. He also points out that I was a person who contributed to that. I am facing a trial here, I'm being prosecuted, and I'm saying that this is true. Outside of this court, I would never confirm this, lest I should be seen to be boasting. Nevertheless, here I can say, as the document states, that the situation definitely improved.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was putting in some good work for 24-hour periods. Why? Because I'm certainly not stupid. As Judge Antonetti says, I'm an educated man. I have a good memory. I have the will. I have the energy that it takes. I have the desire. I rolled up my sleeves, and I did some really hard work. As a result, the situation in Central Bosnia kept improving. And this is an example of a situation like that, to the extent that anything like that was possible, the situation being what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, let's just try to deal with that awkward issue of HV Hrvatintic [as interpreted]. There's a reference here to Nikola Pedjo [phoen] in this document from the Hrvoje Vukcic Hrvatintic [as interpreted] Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Nika, Hrvoje Vukcic Hrvatinic, not Hrvatintic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, but we know that it's an HV brigade because it's mentioned in documents.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an HVO brigade from Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you please explain the circumstances under which 3D0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. General Praljak, in this document, it says - I think it's on page 2 in the B/C/S version, page 3 in English - the behaviour of individuals or groups is mentioned, especially in villages surrounding Prozor, in the Prozor municipality. You remember, General Praljak, that a lot of victims came to testify that they had been ill treated by this famous Kinder Platoon. What did you do at your level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, in Prozor municipality, there are a total of about 60 villages, 60 villages. Anything that goes on, goes on at night. There's always information circulating to the effect that something happened. I have no such information, because I am fighting. But when I arrived, when I receive information, then what happens is I am seized by desperation because you have no way of responding to that or preventing that from happening in an area like that. Anyone physically capable of carrying a rifle is already somewhere along the front-line, defending. That's one thing. You can go and mingle with those people. You can ask them the stupid question, Who did that? But the obvious answer will be -- the answer to be expected will be, None of us did that. The only thing was this: Apart from the SIS trying to investigate and identify a name, the name of a potential perpetrator, and a procedure is instituted, as in any normal country; but the way I worked, the best way to deal with this was to talk with the various bodies that were around, with the senior citizens, with the commanders, as something that might be termed preemptive action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I didn't read out the entire paragraph, in the interests of time, but I must tell you that the author of this report, Mr. Petar Kalinic, added something which is very relevant. He said this: The police was not able to prevent this. But he ended it based on the information they, themselves, committed those acts. So how is it that the military authority, knowing that the police may have caused this criminal behaviour, fails to do anything; does not arrest them, does not arrest all the military policemen involved? Remember, Mr. Praljak, I'm not going to give any names, but we had a witness who told us that this person was taken from prison - I'm not giving you any detail - so the one who wrote this report refers to this type of behaviour, and you were the number one in the military authority. And this military authority is not capable of having law and order prevail in this region. So if you were not able to do so, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first correction: I was not the number-one man of the military police. Please, let's make that clear once and for all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that you were the highest ranking in the military. I said you were the highest with military authority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Units, yes, unit. That's the first thing, but look at what he's saying here. There are certain indications. Your Honours, what can I possibly do with these indications? They have information, they have indications to the effect that someone was busy doing something. First of all, it wasn't the military police in its entirety. There is certain indications that certain military policemen were busy doing something or other. The SIS doesn't have proper equipment. The military police doesn't have proper equipment. They don't go there to find out what the name is, and then they're under an obligation to arrest that person; but say I learn what the person's name is, then I go out and arrest him. But based on what? Indications or indicia? What can I do, based on that? And the indication in this case being here that someone heard something about someone else. Therefore, I assert that it was impossible, regardless of all the effort that went into it, to prevent what was happening in the area at a time like that. No way. I did everything that was within my power to prevent that, but I can't just go out into the street and bring in the first person I come across simply because there are indications. The name is missing. We need a name. There is stuff happening. Well, there is stuff happening in Paris, too, Your Honour; but I'm sure they wouldn't drive you to go and grab the first person in the street and throw them in jail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's not helpful to talk about Paris in this context. Why don't you tell us what you did? You said, I made enormous efforts. What did you do with regard to Prozor or Rama?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I might just intervene at this point. I think there's a misunderstanding, and I had this same feeling yesterday. I apologise if my intervention is not in order, but I think that the first thing is to answer the question of whether somebody was duty-bound to do something or not, and whether someone, with respect to some issue, had any authority to act. Now, in this specific situation is whether one commander, an HVO commander, can do something, anything, if we're dealing with the military police, whether that comes within his chain of command, and whether he is responsible for the conduct and behaviour of the military police. And only once we've ascertained that, that is to say, that the military commander is responsible and duty-bound to take action, only then can we question the witness about what he could and could not do and what he actually did do, because otherwise we're going to ask -- keep asking him about topics that are not within his remit. I hope I've contributed to an elucidation to the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have to comment. You have not really. That was not proper. You have pleaded in between. You have pled, and you have given a lecture on command responsibility to the Chamber, "jura novit curia." You should not have said that, but it has no consequence, of course. Mr. Praljak has just told us, with regard to prohibiting alcohol, that he did things that were not in his competence. Here, a matter was very serious, people are being raped, killed, robbed, but he says, Well, military police, that's not my business. Isn't that so? Isn't that what you tell us? Ms. Pinter, the question was addressed to the witness, and I do not think it's quite proper that you so clearly shake your head and indicate what he should answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak -- one moment. Mr. Praljak, can you answer the question? In your view, does this come under your responsibility or competence or that of the military police? Could you just tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll answer those two questions. First of all, it was not within my competence. That's number one, but let's leave that aside. That's immaterial. I'd like to ask Judge Trechsel not to put something into my mouth which weren't my actual words. I didn't talk about anybody killed, I didn't say that I wouldn't intervene. You asked me what I did. That's what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I did everything in my power, and then I went on to list what that everything was. Now, may I just be allowed to answer, finish my answer? What any human being, faced with a situation like that and attacks, can do to protect 60 villages, what? I'd like to know that. And when you come to judge, I'd like to hear what you would have done, Judge Trechsel, in my place, something that would have been effective, so then I could write another five documents about what should be done. I want to know what could have been done. Nobody could have done more than I did, and I don't believe that you would find any human being anywhere in the world who would have been able to do more than I did, given the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, technically speaking, wasn't it possible at your level to impose a curfew? Secondly, since you had your men in the field, you could have arrested all those that were out on the road at the time of the curfew. This was a solution of a technical nature for any commander in his area. This is a purely technical issue. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no, that was not possible for a number of reasons. First of all, I did introduce a curfew. Secondly, 60 villages are linked up by road, and to block all that off, well, you would need thousands of people to effect a blockade, working 'round the clock in two shifts. And the military police had to go out into the field because it was an enormous offensive, and we were out-numbered fivefold. And if you remember the document from 1992, where I say that a mixed composition should be set up in the villages, well, the assumption that this was not going on was the agreement between the Croats and Muslims according to which some people should be provided with weapons to defend themselves in the villages, because it was clear to every normal human being that criminals would turn up and killers would turn up who'd try and do something and that the forces that Valentin Coric had, or Slobodan Praljak, were not capable of preventing that from happening. So I actually foresaw what was going to happen. It didn't surprise me. To be quite frank, I expected even worse things to happen, because, quite simply, it was not possible to do anything. You didn't have enough men. There were too many villages, too many roads, and the situation had gone on for too long for the people not to break down. And when I say that we had hundreds of talks and discussions, that I didn't go to pick up the remains of my father who had died, but stayed at the meeting, that is something that you can't do through orders. You think I'm illiterate and couldn't have written five order to have them removed from the roads, and that I would have taken a pistol up? I could not have done more than I did do, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we'll change the subject. But by way of a conclusion, should we understand on the basis of your answers, that you were aware of a problem relating to law and order, but that you did not have enough men to face up to this problem? Is that how you would conclude on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that this would happen a year in advance, one year in advance. In November 1992, I said that this would happen. I told them that this would happen, unless the situation was resolved in the way that I had proposed. I said that we would be impotent, we would be powerless, as they were after the Katrina storm and so on. I was just powerless to prevent these things from happening. I was not able to resolve the situation completely. The situation did improve. Now, that it did not improve further, that was not within an individual's power to achieve, not in mine, and I say that there was nobody better placed than me at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, with respect to Judge Trechsel's remark that I was I was nodding my head, I wasn't nodding my head, but the whole document was about -- the whole discussion was about the document 3D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- where there was no mention of, killings, rapes, setting fire to property, and so on. And General Praljak's answer referred to that specific document. But far be it for me that I shook my head and denied something or gave signs or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pinter. I absolutely accept your explanation. Of course, we were thinking of witnesses that we have heard some two or three years ago of this area, and they told us about such event. I'm quite aware that it was not in the document. But please go on. I accept -- I accept your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, when you were in the field, in Prozor, for example, in that territory with the soldiers, did you ever order an attack on a village in which there were civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, come on, Ms. Nika. Please don't ask me that. Come on. These proceedings and this trial isn't at that level.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, I have to ask. Some questions have to be asked. 3D01192 is the next document number. It's one of your documents dated the 31st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It is my document. I signed it, and I demand -- I can't order, I can't issue an order, but I'm requesting that the head of the Defence Department, Mr. Stojic, and Valentin Coric, to replace this gentleman, recall him, because he left the front-line on several occasions without giving any explanation. He did that of his own volition.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Does that relate to Gornji Vakuf, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, Mr. Praljak, I would still like to come back to the question that you did not want to be asked. Have you ever attacked a village? Have you ever given an order to attack a village at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. I never issued an order to attack civilians or anything to do with civilians, and there's so many documents about that. Of course, I defended --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I did not ask that question. I asked whether you ever gave an order to attack a village. I did not speak of civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, some positions of the BH Army -- how do you mean "village"? I don't understand your question. How do you mean attack a village? You don't attack a village. You attack positions of the BH Army. Why would I attack a village if there was nobody there, no soldiers, nothing? Then you don't have to attack. You can just go in, enter it. So I don't really see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is not a dichotomy, as we all know very well, Mr. Praljak. Very often, in villages there are positions. And if you attack the positions, how can you be sure there are not also civilians in that village? I even -- I'm not implying that this is automatically in violation of the laws of war. It may even be not a crime. I was just asking about the fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I attacked BH Army positions. When there was a war between us, then I attacked the positions of the BH Army in front of a village, in a village, next to a village, anywhere where they were, and that is according to war law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you must have taken or -- taken into account and accepted the possibility that there were also civilians? You did not send someone first to evacuate the village, where the enemy positions were, of all civilians? Let me make it clear. You were asked whether you had ever attacked villages where there were civilians. Now, there are two possibilities. One is that you do so on purpose in order to kill civilians, full stop. The other possibility is that you attack a village where there are enemy positions, but possibly or probably also civilians. Then you also attack a village in which there are civilians, although perhaps not unlawfully. So should not your answer to the second eventuality be, yes, that probably, and you may add "unfortunately," may have been the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the case. There's no "unfortunately" about it. The lines were often in front of the first houses. Trenches were dug there. And when you dug at the front-line trenches, there was the possibility of a stray bullet hitting a house, or if you had inflammatory ammunition, that you would set fire to a house. None of that is excluded in this type of situation. But how -- if there happened to be civilians, how am I to evacuate their civilians, if there happen to be any there? Anybody in a war knows that you can't defend yourself and shield yourself by using civilians and that you have to get civilians away from the war zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That was not my question anymore, but I think that we have come a bit more close to what actually happened. Thank you. Excuse me, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the question put by my colleague is an essential question because it refers to several situations in the indictment. Please answer this question fully, because it is crucial if we are to understand what actually happened. I am not going to quote names of villages. I shall discuss with you a theoretical case. That makes it easier for us to understand. Let's assume that you decide to attack a village because the ABiH is in this village. You know they are there, and for strategic reasons you decide to attack this village. Before attacking the village, you organise a meeting with the officers and those people that are going to launch the attack, and you tell them that they should be very careful when they target military targets and they should not target any civilian targets, and you give them very strict instructions and tell them how they should fire their shots. And once the village has been taken, do you give them instructions beforehand on the fact that when the village is taken and people are taken prisoner, then, as part of the Geneva Conventions, the prisoners of war need to be treated properly, and the civilians, women, children and the elderly, should be set aside, since these are not combatants? Is all of this done before the attack so that all the people taking part in the attack have your instructions and orders in mind, and they know what is permitted and what isn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, from the end of March and April 1992, when I first got in touch with the Geneva Conventions and the Red Cross in the Croatian Army, and from that time onwards, I insisted on it every day; not before an attack or after an attack, day after day with all the commanders. That was one of my permanent topics. All the booklets, everything that was done, all the seminars. You will see a document where I deal with the law, and I write to Croatian soldiers that they will be punished and punished to what extent. It was not only before an attack. It was done all the time. It was insisted on all the time. And you saw this footage from Zenica. How they should conduct themselves, not only in a war, but in town, in the street. And when I report this drunken policeman, I'm telling them how things should be from the beginning to the end. Policemen should not be drunk, and least of all, should anyone fire on women and children. So, yes, before every action, it was always drummed into everyone. And this war in Mostar that I claim was waged as if walking on egg shells, we did not want to fire on their positions and their headquarters. It was in the town itself. Every book written on the topic gives me the right to destroy it; yet we didn't do it. And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're telling us, and this is on the record, that you reminded your soldiers of their obligations all the time. This is what you have said, and it's on the transcript. I'm going to fine-tune my question now. We know -- and I'm not going to quote any names of villages, but I can if you like. We know that the defence of these villages was a fairly complex system of defence. Inside the villages, there were houses which had been converted into bunkers, or they had built trenches around the villages in which there were the "fighters," in inverted commas. The problem was that these combatants were oftentimes civilians also. We've heard a number of witnesses testifying to that, and they had to -- these civilians had to go and patrol the trenches when they, themselves, were civilians, and there were ABiH soldiers present. So this was a complex situation. In this kind of situation, let me emphasise that this was an extremely complex situation, did you tell your officers, non-commissioned officers and sergeants, because you said these were the most important men, and I agree with you, did you give them the right instructions? Did you tell them to be very careful about the fact that the civilians and the soldiers could get all mixed up in difficult moments like those? Was this a notion which had been passed on to the soldiers of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things, Your Honour. Civilians are civilians, and this idea was drummed into them. A man with a rifle was a target, and that's what I drummed into them, too. I was there to protect the lives of my troops. My troops didn't have to care whether the person with the gun was a member of the BH Army or not. It was an enemy soldier. The moment you saw that they had a rifle and they're firing on you, they're enemy soldiers. And if they refuse to surrender, they are a target, a regular military target. And I clearly made this distinction for them. So I didn't tell them, Now stop there and think a while, because that would get them killed. I was a commander, and I had to keep my soldiers safe. So there was a clear distinction: Has a rifle, is an enemy soldier, is a target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall fine-tune my question a little further. What you have just told us, everyone is able to understand. I assume that before an attack, your officers and sergeants were supervising or controlling the village with all form or any kind of equipment, like binoculars. When you realise that there was the head of a family who was in a trench, and he was clearly an ABiH soldier because he was wearing camouflage uniform, but his wife and children came to bring him milk and things to eat, and this happened all the time, what instructions did you give the 92-millimetre mortars or the tank located on the hill when the fire was shot? Did you tell your men, Only fire when you are quite sure that there are only fighters there, not the wife who brings the bread and the milk or the child that brings a sweet to his or her father ? Did you give them this kind of instructions or did you trust your men in the field entirely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, first of all, in the time when I was down there, I was in command. We were defending ourselves, and there were no such situations. At the time, we were not out to conquer anything. If we lost a position, we would try to recapture it. For the most part, we were successful and so on, and we didn't go into villages. But let me tell you this. I would not have allowed a mortar to fire at the moment when a woman or a child is bringing food or something to somebody, and the situation is clear and the action has not yet started. But if an action has already started, be it their attack on us, or our attack to recapture an elevation, and mortars are in operation, the infantry is doing their job and so on, if a woman is bringing food to somebody, that would not make me change my plan of attack, because at that time in such a situation, she becomes a member of the armed forces. Regardless of the fact that she's just bringing food to them, she is a member of the armed forces. And I would not expose my soldiers to danger and tell them, Stop firing, because then they would get killed, because then a war would be waged in this way. Women would be sent out, the other side would not fire, and then they would get killed. So I would not consider a woman or a child as a target. They could bring food, and they were not to be targeted. But if an action was underway, hypothetically speaking - but I did not encounter this situation, so I'm giving you a hypothetical answer - I would not have stopped the attack just because women bringing food or ammunition, or anything - we don't know what they were bringing - got involved, because they become an integral part of the army, they are troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are, therefore, telling us that, as far as you are concerned, as soon as an action is underway, if a civilian goes to supply a combatant, then you regard the civilian as part of the armed forces of the enemy armed forces. So this is what you say. It's now on record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely it, yes. And they are defined in this manner under -- well, not only soldiers, but all those taking part in the action or aiding it are considered as the enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, which is to be at 4.00, we have another ten minutes, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please look at document 3D --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already discussed it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters ask the speakers not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D01169. Yes, I've already asked you this question. And I asked you to tell us, why was it necessary for Zarko Tole to write this statement, and what circumstances resulted in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an attack on Mostar launched by the HVO on some -- well, some minor attack in some area, and I received a report about that. And then I asked the chief of the Main Staff, because in our internal organisation of work, he was more in charge of Mostar in the south, I was in charge of Vakuf and Rama, and Petkovic was in charge of the north, Kiseljak and the negotiations. Well, we had this division of labour, and he wrote to me, while I was not aware of the attack, and I did not approve it. So somebody -- after all, not every attack is approved by the commander of the Main Staff or his deputy. Every commander in a war knows what his job is. Brigade commanders, operational zone commanders, are in charge of large-scale actions. Or, rather, large-scale actions have to be approved at the level of the Main Staff, but taking an elevation or improving your tactical position, well, where would we be if one person were to decide on everything? It's simply not how it's done in an army. General Lasic had the right to improve his position in a building, in a street. So I merely asked whether Tole had anything to do with it, and all that, and all of it -- this was more because a couple of people were killed in this action, and it was all pointless and stupid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now we have a document that was discussed at length yesterday, but here you can see who it was sent to, this order of yours that persons who commit disciplinary infractions would serve their prison sentences in the Dretelj Prison. And it is listed here who received it. I think that you should tell us what area was informed - 3D01213 - and why only in that area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because Ante Govorusic, the commander, was relaying my order about where this should be done, and that's P05283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to assist everyone finding the document, instead of 3D02123, as in the record, is it not rather D01213?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since my order was delivered to all the operational zones and to the presidents of the military disciplinary courts, because this was their job, they had to provide the papers, the documents, about who received what sentence. And this order was relayed, my order was relayed, and this is something that has to be done in the army, to the Operational Zone North-Western Herzegovina. So this is just for the operational zone. The others had to do that, too, but we have this document only.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Precisely. Now I would like to ask you to look at document 3D01184. This is the SIS Centre Rama, the weekly report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already done that. Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, this is the 4th of October, 1993. Who received this? It went to the Defence Department, not the Main Staff. What can you tell us about the information contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's sending this to SIS, because that's what Mr. Markesic is, he's an SIS, and he's submitting this to his superior. And he's talking about what he, as an SIS operative -- well, what he sees; that there are gaps between positions. This is as if nobody knew that, apart from him, that the troops leave their positions before their relief comes in. Now we get to the stupid sentences, stupid sentences, and nobody holds them responsible. First of all, that's not true. Secondly, if a unit leaves its position, to hold it responsible in the way in which these people think, well, you can do that if you have another unit and you put this other unit to man the positions and put the other guys in prison for 20 years. But if you see that these people say that they spent 40 days in a trench, and they say, Well, we can't do it. They can't do it. And now they can be members of an army, but they're first of all human beings. They have glassy eyes. They do not function anymore in any form or shape or under any kind of assumption that is always trying to be introduced here, that they are some kind of iron men, machines, and these are just structures, Newtonian mechanical structures, and the only way that evil comes about is when the person moving them does it wrongly, and that's not how it is. If you look at the person who has spent 30 days in a trench, you can tell that guy whatever you like. You can issue any kind of orders whatsoever; that man does not respond to anything, and he does not respond in World War II, in World War I. People simply do not respond. You can only fire at them, and that's it, and you will not do that. And then he goes on to say that there is the possibility of an offensive, whereas the offensive was ongoing at the time. So he is dealing with the soldiers and that makes no sense; that a lot of soldiers are being lost. And then again he says, If no major action is taken as soon as possible -- well, this is a man of high morals, but he is not very smart. He's sitting in his office and he's saying, Well, unless something is done as soon as possible -- well, if we don't do anything as soon as possible, anything serious, the war between the Israelis and the Palestinians is going to go on for centuries, and nobody is going to say what we should do. These are just platitudes, stupid platitudes. If, Ms. Nika, we don't do something serious, millions of children will go on dying of hunger, at the time while, for instance, three billion pounds worth of food are being thrown away into the garbage in Great Britain every year. Of course, we have to do something, but I need to be told what we should do, what is it that we should do? Invent better troops, have a better people, and yet we have what we have? Platitudes, platitudes, platitudes. And then he goes on to say, Well, we will not be able to defend this for long. We managed to defend it in the end. And then he says soldiers from Gornji Vakuf and Rama, it will be difficult to persuade them that Herceg-Bosna is to be defended there. And he says rightly that if they lose their positions, if they go to Croatia, this will be lost. 10 percent will perhaps remain --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the witness is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we shall resume with this document after the break. The tape has run out or is running out. We're going to break for 20 minutes, for the only break today, and then we shall resume until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things before I give the floor back to Ms. Pinter. I was mentioning a document earlier this afternoon. I've got the document with me. This is P00592. So that's one thing. You can read Article 27 in it. Secondly, with regard to time, you have used an additional time of one hour and forty-one minutes, because now we have thirty-seven hours and forty-one minutes in all. Please proceed, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we're still at 3D01184. Was there anything else you wished to add about that document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document states that the military police are not doing their job. The civilian police are finding it difficult to get their bearings. Crime is rife, and so is robbery. This is backed by certain people from the police. There might be disruptions to law and order. Catering establishments are opened up all over the place that are not legal. There is a lot of drinking. The HVO decision on curfew is not being complied with, because there was a curfew that applied. Nevertheless, Ms. Pinter, this is something that is written by an officer of the SIS, the official body in charge of saying who it is that is doing all these things, in charge of naming names, in charge of specifying the offences. This is lip service typical of the sort of society in which we lived. Some people did some something somewhere. It reads "individuals from the military police." Yes, but which individuals? They are duty-bound to track them down, and they are duty-bound to bring these people in and to initiate proceedings against these people. It's their duty, yet they write this, they dispatch this to their own administration here, Look, see, I'm not doing my job. I'm saying anything. This was a very honourable human being. And it's not that this person wasn't trained. I can't believe this person couldn't do it or didn't know how to do it, but this is blah-blah-blah. That's all it is. And here he says, Set up a military police that will be able to carry out all the other orders. Setting up, what exactly does he mean? Are we supposed to give birth to new babies who would then immediately become military policemen? Should we bring them in from Switzerland, from the United States, or what? This was precisely what was so often the case, Let's write up something to indicate that something wasn't working right, and then we'll dispatch this document to someone or other, and then this someone - and we don't know who exactly - should probably do something about this and deal with the situation in some way or another. Start criminal proceedings against those who contributed and are contributed against those again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you are challenging the contents of this document. We don't know Mr. Markesic. He did not testify; therefore, we don't know him. However, upon reading this document, are you -- as you have just done with great care, and so have the Judges, one notes that the author is turning to his authorities to say that there is a real situation that has to be tackled at political and military levels. He then added that criminal prosecution had to be done. He mentioned the issue of deserters, and very relevantly, he said that there must be cooperation with the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, he's opening a series of avenues that are obviously far beyond his level of responsibility, asking his superiors to follow all this up. And you realise that, but you didn't say so. There is a first part, as you noticed, related to crimes committed in Uzdol, where statements were taken, as is mentioned in the first part of this document. But besides Uzdol, this man talks about other situations. You are challenging this. I am interested in knowing who were the addressees were of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
