utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I'm not challenging anything. I know about all of this, in part. Yes, what I'm talking about is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I'm interested in, General. I want you to tell me who this document was to be sent to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He sent this to his own administration, the SIS Administration alone, his own superiors up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is his superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivo Lucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And above Ivo Lucic, whom do we find?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivo Lucic is a department [as interpreted] of the Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or, rather, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; a department within the Department of the Republic of the HZ-HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who is the head of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May we also look at the last paragraph on the last page, "SIS Centre activity plan." It seems, in a way, that Mr. Markesic gives the same answers as you have given, in that he says, We're only in the process of building up, we have no personnel, we have only one car, and so forth. Would you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know Mr. Markesic. He is a highly-moral individual who concealed nothing. He truthfully reported on the situation in his own area. I talked to him once or twice about matters such as these. And whenever he said something like this, I would get quite upset -- maybe not upset, but desperate. I would say, In God's name, Markesic, who? You can't say "certain individuals." Who? Name a name, for God's sake. Or when he says, Work on improving the soldiers' accommodation, where, where is this accommodation to be? Where do you put them up? We'd all like that, but where's the money? Where are the barracks, the compounds, so that we could improve their accommodation? It sounds like a nice thing. Everybody's got a wish list, but that's easy. Everybody can enumerate all the problems, from Pakistan onwards. Everybody knows what the problems are. I knew what the problems were, too. But how do you solve a problem? He says it himself: I don't have enough manpower. I don't have the equipment. I can't do that. That's fine. You can't do that, that's fine. Is he to blame that he can't do it? Well, then, okay, he is to blame, and I'm to blame that I can't do more than I can, but I can't. I spent 20 hours a day working. That's what I did. I couldn't do any more than that, and someone comes along and opens up a catering establishment, pours alcohol to all these people. How difficult is that, in a situation like that, to name names? The staff commander, hopping across the entire area to track people down. I don't know. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When you issued that decision banning alcohol, who was supposed to be implementing that decision?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians. You see, no one had sufficient manpower to see an order like that implemented; the military police along the front-line, the civilian police, who barely existed and had just set up there. It has to be an overall effort, the municipal president, each individual. No one must be left out. You can't impose a structural measure like this, because this is not an ordered society that we are looking at. When you have an order like this, you expect each single individual in their right state of mind, those who tried to reason, at least, but most of them just shied away from this, saying, Let the law deal with that, the military police, Stojic or whoever. Let Markesic deal with that. But he couldn't. He wasn't able to deal with that because he would have required 15 men, at the very least. And he didn't have those 15 men; that simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Can we now please go to 3D01173. The 8th of October, 1993, Commander Ante Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used some of our acquaintances to get Mr. Pavlovic to take over the Rama Brigade. The situation improved greatly as soon as he arrived. He was living in Croatia, but was a native of Rama. He was involved in the war from the very beginning. He was an exceptionally brave fighter, and so on and so forth. Nevertheless, he did stay for a while, eventually. We managed to get him to postpone his resignation. But if you look at the document, you see that everyone wanted to be involved in the brigade; the people from the village of Jurici, Glib, Jaklici, and Uzdol. They're all meddling. They are accusing him of unevenly distributing his orders to commanders. There were clashes between the military police and the Rama Brigade, because the people from the Rama Brigade were saying that the military police were all criminals and thieves. He knows, as I do, that there are certain individuals like that, but you can't just label all of the military police as thieves. There were brilliant fighters among those people, and he states that as well. He says he left his family behind in Zagreb, and that he was now fed up, something to that effect, and that now he would like to go back. He says that, There will be a report that we'll be submitting to the SIS. And who undermined the work of this brigade. Because there were people appearing all the time for all sorts of reasons. There were quarrels in the village between groups, and they were undermining the whole system. He was a splendid lad, and what he achieved was -- raised the level of organisation in that brigade considerably. But he is complaining about the -- the -- all the same matters that we were all complaining about at the time. The situation being what it was, all of our resources were not sufficient. All of our work was not sufficient in order to improve things to a degree that was for some reason was expected. Obviously, I had my expectations, too, and I worked towards that end. Too many things. I was trying to achieve too many things, probably, and one of them is described here really well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This document was not submitted to the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would not have been required. It went straight to the operation zone. It wasn't the Main Staff that would have been the place to gather all these documents. There were many operation zone commanders, but he submitted to the Presidency of the HVO, the politicians, all those that he was seeking assistance from. He was seeking assistance from these people, from the politicians. There were some minor political -- petty political games or rifts, quarrels between villages. And what one needed was assistance from the politicians in order to relieve him from all these stories that he was dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What about the report on those who tried to undermine the brigade, something that was to be submitted to the SIS? Was that perhaps the place where such references were to be included?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now 3D0079 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this report shows that in Rama or, say, Prozor, there was a situation that called for measures to be taken. Indeed, it is said that there are individuals with very recent Mercedes cars, that there is a lot of petrol around, whilst the soldiers have nothing. And those who seem to get rich are members of the military police. I think this is worthy of an investigation, isn't it? My question is, therefore, very straightforward. Were the members of the military police in Rama and Prozor ever arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there in 1994, involved in an incident where people were arrested. I was involved in that, too, and managed to persuade some people to give themselves up of their own free will and be taken to prison, in order to then be prosecuted. As to this, to be perfectly frank, I don't know. It certainly was forwarded to the military police. Nevertheless, even he doesn't really say who these people were. It wasn't just men from the military police, Your Honour. There was a lot of smuggling, and the amount increased as the war wore on. You had to get two trucks full of cigarettes across the entire territory . The profit would amount to millions of marks. Smuggling was a burning issue. We didn't touch upon that here because that is another story. But these items were expensive at the time, and the smuggling business started blooming in a number of different ways. And this led to further confusion among soldiers, because if they were receiving any salary at all, it would, as a rule, not be more than 100, 120 marks; and yet they witnessed people around them turn rich over night. And then what happened was clashes between units that were very difficult to allay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my question was very specific, and you answered that there were people arrested in 1994. Very well, thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I know about 1994 because I was there; but this period, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, can we please move on to 3D00793. The date is the 7th of November, 1993. The document has been exhibited. I will, nevertheless, ask you to explain why this letter was written and under what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, this document came about at a meeting that was held and that I had scheduled, a meeting that I had scheduled. I asked for that meeting to be held. That was the last day of my time in the area. A meeting took place the second-last day, the second-last day, the 7th, at 1800 hours or 1900 hours. All of the commanders attended across the units, all of the relevant commanders, brigade commanders, operational zone commanders. All the names are here, all of them. The meeting was held because of everything that we have been discussing; the disarray, the smuggling, all of that. And all of the commanders were aware of the same thing. The overall situation, in terms of war, in terms of the social situation, the mood that prevailed, the structural situation, the municipal situation, was getting out of hand and causing a lot of chaos. The commanders were no longer able to deal with this. Because of the fact that they were aware of that, aware of the fact of the sheer amount of trouble being caused by all this chaos, lack of structure, smuggling, drunkenness, they wrote a letter to President Mate Boban, the Parliament of the Republic of Croatia, the Government, and the Main Staff. Those of us writing this letter knew exactly what it was about; in order to be able to win or, as I say, not be defeated. And then they go on to state some things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's cut to the chase. There is one essential point in this document. It is item 6. It is the very, very fundamental part. I'm going to read it out slowly: "Establish one and only command line." Why is this stated? Does this mean that there were several lines of command? I mean, when you read a document, you have to really go to the core of the matter, and this is really the essential part of the document. This is in your interests, in the interests of the Prosecution, in everybody's interests; so what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That, Your Honour, means, Judge Antonetti, that there wasn't only my line of command, but as you were able to see in the individual municipality structures, those orders were just not respected. And commanders which wouldn't respect the line, had their support in the municipal structures and you couldn't do anything to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I am not satisfied with your answer because you organise a meeting with all the commanders of these men. This is a high-level meeting, and there is a problem with the line of command. That's what is being said is. This is very important. The officers placed under your command, did they question your command, did they state that they reported to another chain of command which was different from yours, or was that chain of command that reported to the municipalities? You are under oath here. Please say exactly why this was one of the conclusions that was drawn at the meeting. In my mind, this is an essential conclusion. What was the issue discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge, it was said that in implementing certain orders, that they were meddling -- that various other structures were interfering in the work of the army, as you saw a moment ago with that one from Rama, that man Pavlovic from Rama; that quite simply some villages and some disputes dictated what his military structure in the brigade would look like, and he was powerless to do anything. So, among other things here, the civilian authority is asked to be subjected to the government of the republic and not have each and every municipality waging their own policies, and some commanders over there said -- gave examples about how they would stand up to -- well, it's not something you put down on paper in black and white. It was lobbying, Don't go up to that line, don't listen to them, you're going to get killed there, so on and so forth. And then you would have them refuse to carry out orders, just like the example of the person I asked to be replaced; he just ups and goes, leaves the territory, and I don't know who was in charge of him; although at that point in time he was subordinated to me in the operational sense. He had to be up at the line, defence line. So my answer is very clear. Now, all the games that were being played were not made public, and then people wouldn't say, I'm not going to allow that. But this was all under hand. There were all these underhand games being played out behind the scenes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall very quickly find you in my question. You issued an order to one of the commanders who is attending the meeting - I won't quote anyone in particular - to, for instance, attack a village held by the ABiH. So your order is very clear. There is a single chain of command. At that moment, the commander who you're giving the order to will go and see the president of the municipality to tell him, Well, General Praljak has given me this order. What do you think of it? Should I go and attack? Should I not attack? What should I do? Does the commander of the unit provide any feedback and say, Well, I was given the order, but I cannot carry it out because the president of the municipality said this and that? And so what happens, your order gets lost. Were you ever confronted with this kind of situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the way in which you've just put it, Judge Antonetti, no. But in another way, take the example of Livno - and I've repeated this three times already - he's not going to write, I won't allow you to, or, I've been given another warning. And the brigade commanders would listen, but it's not -- it's the battalion commanders that aren't listening, and it's all under-hand. Nobody's going to say, Refuse to obey Praljak's orders, what do we care about what he says. But they go 'round lobbying, and then a battalion says, I don't want to go. And you saw a document where that man Vucica arrived in Vakuf, said that I and Filipovic were saying stupid things and sending him to certain death, and he goes home and reports to his battalion. He refuses to obey orders. So somebody was in charge of him in another way, not by issuing a chit, a piece of paper saying, Don't obey Praljak. It's a very under-hand game, behind the scenes. And then I can't do anything to him, because telephones start working, who appointed him, and, If you replace him, we're not going to fight, and things like that. Everything was far more subtle, but there was not one single chain of command, not one command line. Yes, I will try to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, looking at this document and bearing in mind your comments on roughly similar previous documents, I wonder whether this is not just another example of blah-blah-blah: Good intentions put cheaply on paper. What were the consequences? What happened? Did that have any effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we enumerated here and said that the government was meeting all the time, they were holding meetings all the time; Friday, Saturday, Sunday. That was immaterial. The government worked eight hours a day, and I have nothing against that. And some people on Saturday and Sunday would go to the seaside to bathe, to swim in the sea, for instance. Now, furthermore, President Boban quite simply -- and it's stated quite simply here; to abolish the municipality staffs which had rallied together an enormous quantity of divergent, and I think Prlic had a lot of problems with it. That is to say, people who had their separate political interests and every other kind of interest. And it was my proposal -- our proposal, my proposal, that Boban should abolish that because we had a war on, and that he should appoint a commissioner of the government, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, in every municipality; and to say to them, This is war. I'm going to suspend all this wheeling-dealing, and I'm appointing one man, and he's going to be responsible. And you say that point 6 is the material point, but I say that the key point is point 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you are now commenting on this text. My question is a different one. What happened, actually? Was this done? Were the commissioners instituted? Were the command lines secured as one, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, as I've said this is the 7th of September [as interpreted], in the morning. So I can't answer that question, and I can't comment on this text, because the text, after a discussion, was compiled and written with my vital participation in it. And the key point was point 2 for further developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Thank you. It actually confirms, more or less, for our purposes. What we see here is a piece of paper with nice plans and intentions, full stop. By the way, it was the 7th of November, not September, as was stated in the transcript on page -- on line 11. Excuse me, Ms. Pinter, but I wanted to finish this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague also drew my attention to point 2. One of the essential items was item 6, but item 2 may be of interest also. Clearly, you seem to be asking that a commissar be appointed in each municipality to do away with staff municipalities, so to speak. There are crisis staffs and war staffs in each municipality. Over these last three years, I have felt - this is a feeling I have had and not a conviction - that the local rulers played a considerable role. Let me take the case of Mr. Topic in Mostar. If your second proposal had been carried out in Mostar, does this mean that Mr. Topic would have no role to play anymore? In that case, it is a commissar of the government that would be playing this role. So this is my question: Since you exercised command, did you have the feeling that the local elected officials, when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was created in Grude, did -- were you under the impression that these people were very powerful people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. They had some money from abroad coming in. Well, some municipalities more, others less, so they could influence the army through salaries. They were powerful, but that was untenable. You couldn't work like that anymore. So these are demands. They're not requests. They're precise demands, demands of the government, telling it how it should function, what to do to reorganise. And along the lines of what I've been saying all the time. You had to change the political and social structure, because otherwise you couldn't improve army establishment because the foundations were bad. You would build this building and then the Tower of Babel would fall down because the construction, the ground work wasn't good. You had to put everything on firmer ground, firmer foundations. So you didn't know who was doing all this. Everybody would say, It wasn't me, it was him, and so on. And it was just a fishing expedition, or you could see that it was -- that it wasn't working properly. Whereas if you knew that it was one man, then you would know who that man was, and if something went wrong, then Mate Boban could replace that person; whereas he had 10 or 15 people in every municipality who represented the powers that be, and each one of them would employ somebody from his own family and wouldn't want to send them to the front. So they'd employ them in the Customs officers or wherever just to prevent them from going to the front-lines, and this would give rise to rebellion. You would have 60 or 70 guys saying, Look at what they're doing over there? Are we going to go to war for that kind of thing, whereas I have to go and fight and defend the country for 120 German marks? Well, I'm not going to do that. They say, No, we're not going to do that. So the problem was far greater, and we have set out precisely where the problem lay in these points here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just a note for the transcript. The time after this meeting on the 7th of November, Witness Biskic testified about that. And through his evidence and documents on the 6th of March, 2007, and through his evidence, you could see whether there were any results after this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, now I would like you to look at 3D01175. It's a document dated the 8th of November, 1993, from Uskoplje, Pero Pilic. It's a report to the Main Staff, to the sector for I don't know what -- Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the documents, Ms. Pinter, are like peas in a pod here. We've already a talked about that. Well, he says in Zrinski, the lack of manpower has reached a critical point. People are leaving the line the way they see fit. The morale is low. They -- as if they don't care for anything. Fatigue results in total numbness, and the result -- this is the result of the fact that they have spent only four or five days out of the previous month out of the trenches. I would like all of us here in the trial to -- participating in this trial to spend at least two nights in a trench in the winter-time at really low temperatures, and we would all be able to understand this problem so much better. To spend 30 days in a trench would break the stoutest fellow. And they no longer care whether they're alive or dead, where they're going, what's happening. Soldiers are human beings, human beings, and these are not people who were trained to be tough. They were farmers, they raised cattle, they were locksmiths, and so on, metalworkers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We've done -- we're done with this file. We've agreed that we would -- do you want a document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Where is the report, the report that I have? Well, it's in another --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's in the next binder, and that's documents by way of explanation, documents to explain. But before we move on to this binder, you said that you wanted to show the video from Prozor when you talked about the man who came to demand money from the president of the municipality. The number for the video, 3114. The transcript has been handed to everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Praljak, give me the money. The money, give me the money. "Wait, wait, tell me. What money? "They burnt my house down. Give me the money. "Wait, wait, wait. Tell me, who burnt your house down? "You know very well who that was. Give me the money. Fill it up. "Okay, let us agree. Easy there. Calm yourself down. We will find a solution. Now let me hear about it. Who burnt your house down, who? "You know damn well who. "Here's the thing, you want the money, the money. Well, I'm not giving you the money. I'm not giving you the money. I will not give you the money. Take him away. Take him away. Get out."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, did this actually happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; not just once. That's what it looks like. We're talking about things from a great height, at some rarified heights, and this does not -- that's not what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: For the record, this man came into your office with a gun and asked for money for his house that had been burnt down?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yeah. He first went to the brigade commander. Jozic had a breakdown after that. That was the fifth or sixth case of that kind. He left for Germany. He had a breakdown, and, of course, he had it, a break down. He never came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Pinter. I would only like to ask Mr. Praljak how it happened, when that person came in, you had already there a television team, because it was anyway taken either by television or by other kind of -- other person, if he had this -- any way to be already prepared to take it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prandler, this was not taken by a TV crew that was there. But based on the documents that are here, a report about this event and witness testimony that has been submitted to this Trial Chamber, well, I filmed -- I made a film, a feature film, of this event. It is a realistic depiction, a reenactment of the actual events. So this is not an authentic -- this is not authentic footage. This was done afterwards, but in a documentary manner. It's like the previous video from Travnik that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Mr. President, the transcript indicates -- well, could we get the exhibit number for this last piece of video because I think the number in the transcript is not correct. We want to be sure to object to the correct exhibit when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D03114. The transcript pertains to Rama 1993. It says "Transcript number 1."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, now we are at the set of the documents that we entitled "Documents to Explain," including three presidential minutes from the office of the president. So I would like you to go first to document P00147. The minutes have already been exhibited, and I would like you to go to page 01863800. It is page 23 of 37 in the translated version. That's for the benefit of the Chamber and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this transcript mostly deals with the Croatian Army in April 1993. For the most part, it pertains to an attack in Baranja and the responsibility of the commander who was later removed from his post. And at that page, when the president gave me the floor -- well, this just gives you an idea about my frame of mind, the way I was thinking, that this mistake by the commander was a major mistake, because before that they were all in President Tudjman's office, and they had been prohibited from engaging in any kind of offensive action. And this was no tactical action, such as you have in a war. It was an action that was not to be taken. And then I go on to say that there was a problem with responsibility, and I say that every successful army has to remove commanders if they do not do their job properly. And in order to see whether they do their jobs properly, I say that an analysis of the actions should be done, because a lot of time has passed already, and an analysis of an action that resulted in failure, with a great number of casualties couldn't perhaps be done while the fighting was going on. You had to wait until the cease-fire in January 1993, but after that it had to be done. I know about this action that was taken by 102 Brigade. They crossed the River Kupa. It was close to where I was. A lot of people were killed because the commanders of battalions and companies at lower levels remained at one bank, and they sent the troops to cross to the other bank, and that was inadmissible. And I say that it is not that heads should roll, or anything of the sort, but this is not something 4 that should be brushed under the carpet. Those people who didn't do their 5 job well secured certain positions for themselves in the HV and this is not 6 good because it affects the combat readiness of the Croatian Army. when the troops see that the commanders remained at their posts after such a botched action, they will not follow them into action tomorrow, because people know very well -- the troops know the quality of their commanders. And if it's a commander who will stay behind the lines, 10 kilometres behind the lines, and since I had been in Herzegovina before that, Mr. Nikolic, who was the commander at the time of all of that, he was totally inept, he didn't know. And as I said, you could learn more from the radio about what the fighting was and what it looked like than from that man. He didn't know anything. Fortunately, he was replaced, and then after a while General Petkovic was appointed there. So that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, well, a suggestion from my colleague. The action was in Bosnia and Herzegovina or in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the Republic of Croatia. We're talking about the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, the transcript does not reflect that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, well, they say that the commission was set up, and General Bobetko was in the commission, so was General Spegelj and myself, and we did this job; and General Gorinsek was replaced because he was not doing his job properly. This was not how things were to be done. At page -- at page 01363810 -- 01363810, and Ms. Pinter, you could perhaps say -- give us the English reference --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, this will be a bit difficult. 137 -- 3237, I'm sorry. No, yeah, it's my mistake. I didn't prepare the English. Okay, you go on, and I'll find it in the document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just talking about what I said here. Well, there was a lot of talk about this action because there were a lot of casualties. And it was my demand that a press release be issued about what happened, who made the mistake, and who was replaced. So -- and I say here, and I quote: "So a press release, which would be loud and clear, would do away with all the rumours that surround this," and so on and so forth, "for the commanders to know that they are not to do this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That they should not do --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they should not do this kind of thing, so that there should be a press release.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the page is 32 of 37, that's in the English language, or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the counsel please slow down when reading numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IT0186-3779 to 0186-3815. The page is 32 out of 37.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as regards this document, well, everything is in there. President Tudjman clearly indicated that his decision was already made and that the commission could only recommend the sentence that is to be expected or the punishment that is to be expected. And then there was a debate about whether he should appear in public or not. He had already spoken out in the media. And it was decided that he should not speak to the media from that time onwards. And I said that he should not have spoken in the media as he had. As a general of the Croatian Army, he should have sought approval from his chief of Main Staff, and that was General Tus, for any public appearances. And people thought that they could do whatever they want, present their political views, that Serbs should be attacked in this way or in that way, and that was one of the reasons why I demanded that Gorinsek should be removed from office.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The next document is P00466. It's also been exhibited. These are the minutes from a meeting held on the 11th of November -- 11th of September, 1992. These are the minutes that are mentioned in the indictment. This is the National Defence Council meeting, and, General -- P00466. Could you please go to ERN page 0186-2960. 0186-2960. The English version is page 50 of 64, because the ERN numbers are all the same. And at that page and the page that follows, there is discussion, and now I would like you to tell us something about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Pinter, I am opposed to removing -- well, this is an important meeting where a number of things were discussed. So as a professional, as a professional director, I can do anything you want from quotes. So this meeting has gone on for a certain period of time and important topics are discussed. I will not be making references to exact pages, but I will tell you, as a participant, what was discussed. So it's a document. The president of the state is talking about how the combat disposition should be such that it could be deployed in peacetime. And then he says that there would be some resistance to the implementation of the UNPROFOR mandate, of course, on the part of the local Serbs, and that there would be some resistance to the Croatian constitutional order in that area. And then he talks to the interior minister about problems with the HOS that existed in Zagreb. And he's angry because this has not been resolved fully. They are walking around Croatia with their weapons. Then President Franjo Tudjman asks himself how is it possible that in a state that has a rule of law, that somebody from the HOS is in a position to sign some documents where a politician, a member of a political party, claims that he is the Commander-In-Chief of an armed force. This person was also a member of the Parliament. He was elected into the Parliament. But this had to have been dealt much more firmly, and in the end it was. President Tudjman says that there is no need to fool ourselves, because the foreign intelligence services will continue working against the Croatian state and that one should not be naive there; that the position of the Republic of Croatia has improved greatly. He mentions that there have been some changes in the French policy, but that the military component will definitely be of interest to the intelligence services. Then he goes on to say -- goes on to speak about the military council. Well, Minister Susak says that half of the military council went out into the field. I talk about the defence industry here at the beginning that exists in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Herzegovina, and that somebody should be appointed the coordinator, who would -- a coordinator between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, who would act as a mediator. Then I speak about this major problem, and the problem is this: When the Croatian Army was being demobilised, it was being cut down to 50.000 people, and a lot of people had to be demobilised to reach that -- to reach that number of people. That was the demand made by the president of the state, and many people who were demobilised had their own weapons. And because they were in dire straits financially, they sold those weapons, and, in most cases, they sold those weapons to members of the BH Army. There were soldiers, Muslims, who at that time were buying weapons, and this resulted in the black market. There was no control. Then he talks about the serious problem of how to obtain weapons, whether it should be done through the Defence Ministry. Minister Susak says that an agency should be set up, that all Western countries have something of the sort. General Imra Agotic says that in Mostar, in Sokol, there is the -- of course, the repair and maintenance facility for aircraft and that Libya wanted to repair some of its planes there, do the maintenance there. And then Libya also wanted us to work on some of their vessels because those vessels were actually made by Yugoslav shipyards in Tito's times. And there was also a big problem because at that time people who were expelled from UNPA zones were exerting a lot of pressure on the government and the president. There was peace for quite some time, but they wanted to go back to their homes, and they were ready to use force to do it. There were tens of thousands of people who wanted to do that. It was a major political problem. So there was this discussion about what would happen if they moved, if they start to advance. And I claim that if they headed into Posavina, that the Krajina army would fire on them. And then at one point I say that unfortunately the situation in the Croatian Army is not good for a number of reasons and that this plan for the return of people, without any prior preparations, would result in a major bloodbath. Dr. Franjo Tudjman is forever hoping that the situation -- well, that the Serbs would have to forego the war, fighting. He says that they would have to calm the situation down to avoid the escalation. He saw the Vance-Owen report where, well, everybody's hoping. And then he goes on to say, Okay, we never did stupid things, and we will not do stupid things now. We will not let people go there without organising things. Then the president says that -- he tells us how much Croatia earmarked for its armed forces, and he says that when the next agreement will be reached with UNPROFOR, he will demand that the road through Okucani should be opened, that's Croatia, that the Maslenica Bridge should be opened. That's again Croatia. It's important, well, to clear up the situation in Bosnia, and he's hoping that the Serbs have no other solution but to forego aggression. He has information to the effect that the climate is changing in the talks. Dr. Jure Radic, who was his Chief of Staff, speaks about the decision of the working group in Geneva, and he says that the London Conference is considering the whole situation, the whole crisis in the former Yugoslavia. And he says, explicitly, the neighbouring countries involved in all this, that's Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he says that a working group for Bosnia and Herzegovina has been charged with working on the cessation of hostilities and the constitutional solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina. And now we can, yes, move -- well, there is always talk -- he goes on to say that Croatia demands that direct or indirect aid be curbed to neighbouring countries. And Dr. Radic says that the United Nations, pursuant to a decision of the London Conference, should establish their observers between Bosnia and Herzegovina; well, he says Bosnia and Serbia and on the Bosnian-Montenegrin border, to have international control of the borders, and that heavy weapons would be deployed, or placed, as it was thought, under the control. It was the eleventh hour for the war to be stopped, under the control of the United Nations. Dr. Tudjman talks about the fact that Croatia is facing a very delicate situation. If they stick to the letter of the law on those resolutions, Croatia should withdraw all aid to Bosnia and Herzegovina. He says "by intervention," but when he says "intervention," he means assistance, the heavy weapons, the volunteers as well, in order to thus stop the possibility. He says this is a delicate situation, and this is about the cooperation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO along Croatia's borders. And he says that this is a delicate situation between the Croatian leadership and the Bosnian leadership. Because Mr. Izetbegovic, following the London meeting, visited him in Zagreb, saying he wanted to press on with the war. Therefore, Izetbegovic and Silajdzic were not considering a cessation at all, yet they were expecting to receive further supplies from Croatia and through Croatia. He then goes on to mention the fact that a plane from Iran landed, carrying some medicines, but a lot of weapons too. I know about that. I was involved, personally. The president says that he informed the UN about this, and UNPROFOR as well, and the US government. He's also conscious of the fact that the intelligence services knew everything --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. The transcript is in evidence, and I think we're just wasting time having the general paraphrase what's being said by the various participants. He's not adding anything, so we're just really wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't agree. I don't think this is a waste of time, simply because the transcript was part of the indictment to incriminate General Praljak. He was at this meeting, and it is claimed that his words at the meeting contributed to certain claims made in the indictment. This is a meeting attended by General Praljak. The fact that this is an exhibit does not mean that it shouldn't be evaluated. It is yet to be evaluated and its probative value established. In order to be able to d that, you have to hear General Praljak, who attended that meeting, and who has to explain the words that he uttered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, it is right to say that this document is part and parcel of the pre-trial brief, since it is quoted, and I had every intention of using it when I put my questions. On the other hand, Mr. Stringer is right to say that this document has already been admitted. It would be better, rather than Mr. Praljak read the document, which we are familiar with, that you put questions to him on the essential questions you wish to demonstrate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the document is admitted, as far as I am concerned, there is nothing relevant here. As far as I'm concerned, at the meeting, I spoke about the problem of refugees, Muslims expelled by the Serbs, who were now settling in areas where, prior to the outbreak of the aggression, there were equal amounts of both Croats and Muslims. My proposal at the time was this, and I haven't changed my proposal to this very day: I knew it was fictitious, and that it would come to nothing, but I just wanted to send the buzz around so everyone starting thinking about it. I was saying that the refugees in Croatia, both Croats and Muslims, because Croatia - in my understanding of international law - was a party to the war. And being a party to the war, Croatia was in no position to receive refugees. Refugees were to be received by countries that were neighbours to the conflict. My proposal at the time was that all the refugees be sent to Western Europe. Why? Because I was claiming at the time, and I still am, as a matter of fact, that whenever one is trying to come to grips with a problem, you're having a hard time, no one else understands, no one else cares. Had the refugees been sent to Germany, France, or England in numbers that would have exerted pressure on their respective governments, it is my belief that the assistance to our efforts to resolve the conflict in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina would have been much greater. Unfortunately, I know full well that this was not do-able. It was just a theory that I had, a fiction, if you like. If I'd been able to see it implemented at the time, I would have taken every step necessary, though, simply because had that been the case, people would have seen the light much sooner. They would have realised what this was all about, and they would have realised the high cost entailed. They would have started worry about their own finances. The reaction would have been different, and the war would not have gone on until 1995. This way, all the casualties, and dead, and the wounded were nothing more than dead figures on a piece of paper. The refugees were but a figure on paper. Everything is just a figure on paper. Every now and then something happens that takes on a symbolic value; the explosion at the Markale market in Sarajevo, little Irma on her way to London, as well as the refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer is right in saying that we shouldn't waste our time. In this document, I shall get back to it at a later stage, I wanted to tell you this -- well, finish and then I will tell you something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done with this document, Your Honour. I expect questions from the Prosecutor and from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one question, but I will get back to this later. On the English version, on page 56 and following pages, at one point the Banovina is mentioned, and Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina are mentioned. There is a dialogue between you two, between Tudjman and Susak. And Tudjman makes it clear that nothing should be done and nobody should move. And you say on page 57 of the English version: "No, Mr. President, believe me, the attacks have been stopped." And Susak follows up on this by saying, "Nothing in the Banovina, not even one metre." So clearly there is no question of doing anything whatsoever for the Banovina. This could be of interest, if we are discussing the joint criminal enterprise. Do you remember ever having discussed this during this defence council meeting? Prominent figures were presented and attended this meeting. Mr. Mesic was there. He was then in capacity as the president of the Parliament. There were all those people that have been quoted in the indictment as having taken part in the joint criminal enterprise. Some other people are not mentioned, but well-known names, like that of General Cermak and you, figure in this document also. And you play an important part, since you take the floor on several occasions. Now, as far as this particular issue is concerned, the Banovina, can you tell us what Tudjman's position on that was on that day, what Susak's position was, and what your position was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, the situation is crystal clear in that respect. The Banovina means nothing here. It is no more than a geographical notion related to Eastern Herzegovina. The Banovina, as far as that's concerned, if we set aside Croatia, because the Banovina belongs to Croatia too, was set up to counteract the power of the king in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, in various -- with a Croatian majority. Franjo Tudjman is saying here, Defend that area in Bosnia and Herzegovina in which the Croats and the Muslims, too, were a majority. And, Praljak, don't move on Nevesinje and Trebinje because the Serbs are there. General Bobetko then goes on to say, But if we don't go in just ever so slightly, into Bosnia-Herzegovina, we shall never liberate Croatia South and Prevlaka. And then Tudjman says, We'll take that back when there is peace. Please don't go in there. The Banovina here has no legal or constitutional meaning. What is going on here is Tudjman is saying, Don't launch any attacks when peace is here. We shall resolve the whole thing. And then I said, We won't, we won't. President, don't worry. And then we laughed a little and all that. At this point in time, we are in Stolac, and we stopped right there. It's about the president saying, Don't move further from there. Don't launch a defence war. We defended all the areas from Republika Srpska and from the JNA, the Muslim and Croat majority areas, and stop right there. These are the facts of the matter, and that's as clear as a spring day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask this question: When you say, and these are your own words, "No, Mr. President, believe me, the attacks have been stopped," when you say this, you are saying this to reassure Mr. Tudjman, who a few moments before, according to the English document I have, that he is not concerned by conquering Bosnia. But when you say that the attacks have been stopped, what attacks are you actually alluding to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO, Your Honour, near Stolac. I was there, and I spoke about that. But then General Tus says, One cannot defend Dalmatia if you're not across the border. We're talking about this damn belt that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Army of Republika Srpska. There are no clashes with the Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, all right. Let's take it easy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjo Tudjman says, We shall not take anything in Bosnia. You won't cross the border with the Croatian Army at all. And what we're looking at here is the HVO. Will the HVO go beyond Stolac at all towards Nevesinje and Trebinje, further into Bosnia-Herzegovina's territory? And then he says, Don't fight anymore. We shall take back Prevlaka when peace is back. That's what it says. And then I say, All right, that's it. If we do anything, in the military sense, about Prevlaka, without Nevesinje or Trebinje, nothing can be done. And the president replies by saying, Yes, that is clear to me. But then he also says that Prevlaka shall be ours when peace is back. That's what I wrote down. He says, Listen, let's be realistic. We just barely avoided having sanctions imposed on us by the world and the Islamic countries. If we and those who are the aggressors in Bosnia, taking territory in Bosnia -- all right, there you have it, that's the problem that -- that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this part of the text is important. Any reasonable trier of fact would have this question. On that day, was there something of a hidden agenda between you two? People were saying things and nobody believes it, or was there actually -- what happened at the time, or was there no question for a second of invading Bosnia and Herzegovina? If Mr. Mesic had come, had he been a neutral participant, we would have put the question to him. We are putting the question to you now, because you are a witness. What we can see in this document, this is a conversation between several people. All these people are high-ranking people. What all these people are saying is: Does this match reality or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fully, Your Honour, fully. We pulled important positions in that country. How on earth would we end up telling lies to each other in a closed meeting like this behind closed doors? This was a perfectly sincere, outspoken conversation. But you must know, no country in the world with a document like this ever sees the light of day because of the nature of these meetings. There's no single country in the world that would ever accede a document like that to anyone, for at least 50 years after the fact. Therefore, what is there to conceal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is another presidential transcript. I can't give you the number now because I had not intended to ask you this question. But just to compare things, I am now led to tell you this: At some point in time, Tudjman explains to the people taking part in the meeting that there are public and secret agreements with Izetbegovic. And he said this: I quote from memory, but you can trust me on this, There is going to be a union or republics in a form of a confederation, that's what he says, and then he adds this: Abdic, the famous Fikret Abdic, is going to make sure that he's going to secede so that the territory he has be incorporated into Croatia. So that is what Tudjman says. What do you think of this? What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the territory under Abdic's control was meant for the Serbs. Tudjman had been hoping that Abdic -- this thing about this being annexed by Croatia, I simply can't bring myself to believe that. It may be something that someone wrote at the time, but you're about to see something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll show the document. I can guarantee that Tudjman said this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what's written, that he said it, but I'm always adamant all these jokes that we were exchanging, let's move on, let's not move on, one thing that was clear is that we would not be moving on. There is no irony. If you look at this written on a piece of paper, you can't see the tone, you can't see the general atmosphere. Errors are possible, too. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I ran against President Tudjman at the first presidential election in Croatia, and I had been with him for a long time. It never even crossed Tudjman's mind that he would be reaching for any part of territory that was outside Croatia's borders, unless the Americans so decided and all the other great powers. In the next transcript, you will see when he starts saying, You don't understand what Eagleburger is saying, and you don't understand this, and you don't understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you, since we have little time left. But you said something important, and I had not quite thought of it. This territory controlled by Fikret Abdic, based on what you say, was occupied by the Serbs. Is this territory part of the Republika Srpska today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The best part, yes. There was a part that wasn't, and there was a part that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And is there a small part of this territory that is now part of the federation back then of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was a part like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you didn't know at all that at some point in time, in having Mr. Abdic seceding, he would attach himself to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't know that. But regardless of the fact that the reference to this may be written somewhere, Your Honour, there were 500 statements by Franjo Tudjman, and 500 statements written up. Something may have been there by mistake. He may have misspoken, but he never truly believed or thought that anything like that might happen. We have to be realistic, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it was not an error, if it was the truth, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have said what all the international evidence indicates. If the internationally-recognised borders by the UN were to be changed, they could only be changed by agreement between the two interested parties. If Abdic had been granted statehood in his territory, if he had been granted statehood, if the people that he led by his consent and the consent of the Croatian authorities, with the appropriate legal procedure, had opted to join Croatia, I would have gone along with that. Again and again, what I'm saying is this: The only way borders can be changed or altered is by an agreement between the relevant parties, under the UN laws and decisions, and so on and so forth. Our project of Croatia was not yet completed. How can anyone possibly be reaching for another's territory when there is a third of his own territory that is still under foreign occupation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, you have another eight minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, General, I have to ask you, just to dispel any doubt, because you were speaking too fast. When we spoke about Bihac, part of Bihac became part of Republika Srpska, the Bihac area, not the city itself; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the best part of the area became part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And part of Bihac was --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Became part of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We have only little time left. Perhaps we should conclude this document, because the presidential transcripts might take some time. Maybe we should move on to something that we can deal with faster just in order to wrap it up by the close of business today. My colleague is advising me to ask you this: Whose idea was the idea about a confederation between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was an American idea. It's not that I'm thinking. I actually know, with sure and certain knowledge, that this was something that came from the Americans. It was a demand that they made for a federation to be set up, and then and then this should join Croatia in the form of confederation. It struck me as entirely unintelligible, because the Republika Srpska would then enter a confederation with Serbia, and then Serbia would be in a confederation with Croatia. It simply boggled the mind. Unless one wanted to allow Republika Srpska to become a part of Serbia, with the two states remaining. But whoever was in charge of constituting the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in a confederation with Croatia, the only way for them to survive would have been by carving up Bosnia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and keep it from existing as a single state. Republika Srpska could only have existed at this time as a part of Serbia, simply because no one could have stopped it becoming a part of a confederation with Serbia. And then within the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a federation, which is then a confederation with Croatia, no one ever came up with anything like -- that is something that cannot be. You, after all, are lawyers, and you know that such a thing can never exist. It begs belief. There were other interests concealed behind this, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I suggest that we now move on to an effective control document, what might have been an effective control document. But it's here because it's an exhibit already. The document number is P05530. The date is the 1st of October, 1993, a field report from the assistant commander of the 1st Motorised something or other, I don't know what the abbreviation stands for, political activity, Mato Prce?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Would you just please tell the Chamber why this document is important, and can you please explain that, what the document is about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. We've got five minutes left. You can ask away later on, but what this document says is that there were volunteers from the 5th Guards Brigade. And it talks about how many of them were killed, what exactly they did, and so on and so forth. What I'm looking at, and what I believe is important to point out, and I think I can manage to do that in the following five minutes: At the end of page 2 of the Croatian document - I'm not sure about the English reference - it says that the column, on its way back into Croatia, was stopped at the toll booth in Karlovac - Karlovac is just south of Zagreb - pursuant to an order of General Slobodan Praljak, an HVO commander. They had been accused of robbing houses in the Uskoplje front. The police inspected the column and found a freezer, a fridge, a TV set, and an oven in a person's vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The page number is 5 in English, 5 out of 6.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, what I'm trying to say is this: The people from that brigade, who, prior to that, had been involved in the fighting from the very start of the aggression against Croatia, were, for the most part, from the Vukovar front. They survived their ordeal there. Their families are either dead or living elsewhere, displaced. They went there as volunteers, in smaller numbers than is normally reported, because there's a lot of dispersion going on all the time, obviously. There was this once I was dealing with Mr. Leko's group. They spent 43 consecutive days in a trench. And I'm now telling all the lawyers here, the Honourable Chamber, and the OTP, had I reported those people, then I might as well have gone on to report my own father and my own brother. Nothing was ever more difficult for me to do than that. It was the hardest task ever faced. Those people had either purchased these items or whatever. They were displaced. Maybe they took a fridge or something. It is true, it is not the done thing. Nevertheless, having been through all that, the fierce fighting, everything that they contributed after Vukovar, reporting these people and besmirching their reputation, it was heart-rending for me. And I had a splitting headache at the very thought. It was an awful thing to do. Nevertheless, I didn't stop at that. I reported them, and again I would have reported anyone in any situation in which I was aware of anything untoward having happened, but I would rather have faced the choice of reporting my own brother as opposed to these lads here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to stop now. We have taken due note of what you have said. We're going to resume next week with this binder, because we still have a few documents in it that we haven't seen, and in principle on Monday you should finish your examination-in-chief. And then we'll have a break, at your request, on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. And then we'll be very glad to see Mr. Stringer again on the week after that, and then I'll start with my questions. So this is the schedule for the coming days. Thank you. See you on Monday. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
